steps.text: Radical halogenation is a **chain reaction**. **Initiation**: light (hν) splits Br2 into two Br•. **Propagation**: Br• takes an H from the alkane (giving H–Br and R•), then R• takes Br from Br2 (giving R–Br and a new Br•). **Termination**: two radicals meet and pair up, ending the chain.
Which of these is a **propagation** step?

options.explains: Right. A radical goes in and a radical comes out, so the chain keeps going.
That's initiation: radicals are made from a molecule with no radicals.
That's termination: two radicals combine and none are left to carry the chain.
Also termination. It uses up two radicals and makes none.

steps.text: Radicals, like carbocations, are stabilized by alkyl groups: **3° > 2° > 1° > methyl**. Allylic and benzylic radicals are even more stable, because resonance spreads the unpaired electron over several carbons. A more stable radical means a weaker C–H bond, so that H is removed fastest.
Br• removes an H from 2-methylbutane. Tap the carbon whose H it takes.
steps.explain: C2 is the only 3° carbon. Removing its H gives the most stable (3°) radical, and Br• is very selective for it.

steps.text: **Br2 is selective; Cl2 is not.** Per H, Br• prefers 3° : 2° : 1° roughly 1600 : 80 : 1, but Cl• only about 5 : 4 : 1. So with Cl2 the number of each kind of H matters, and you usually get a mixture.
With 2-methylpropane, Br2/hν gives almost only tert-butyl bromide, but Cl2/hν gives more 1-chloro-2-methylpropane (about 64%) than tert-butyl chloride. Why the difference?

options.text: H abstraction by Br• is uphill, so its transition state looks like the radical and feels the 3° radical's stability; Cl• reacts fast and early and barely tells the H's apart.
options.explains: Right (Hammond postulate). With Cl•, the nine 1° H's outnumber the one 3° H and win on statistics.

options.text: Cl• forms a 1° radical because 1° radicals are more stable.
options.explains: 1° radicals are the least stable. Cl• gives mostly the 1° chloride only because there are nine 1° H's and one 3° H.

options.text: Cl2 reacts through a carbocation, Br2 through a radical.
options.explains: Both are radical chain reactions started by light. The difference is how selective the halogen atom is.

options.text: Br2 is bigger, so it can only reach the 3° hydrogen.
options.explains: The 3° H is actually the most hindered. Br• prefers it because of radical stability, not size.

steps.text: **NBS** (N-bromosuccinimide) brominates the **allylic** position of an alkene. The allylic C–H is weak because the allylic radical is resonance-stabilized. NBS reacts with HBr to release Br2 slowly, keeping it at a very low concentration, so Br2 addition across the C=C can't compete with the radical chain.
Cyclohexene with Br2 in CH2Cl2 gives trans-1,2-dibromocyclohexane. With NBS and light it gives 3-bromocyclohexene. Why the switch?

options.text: NBS keeps the Br2 concentration tiny, so polar addition to the C=C is too slow and the radical chain at the weak allylic C–H wins.
options.explains: Right. Addition needs Br2 to form the bromonium ion; at very low [Br2] the radical substitution takes over.

options.text: NBS is a nucleophile that attacks the C=C.
options.explains: NBS is a source of Br (Br2 and Br•), not a nucleophile; the succinimide part doesn't end up in the product.

options.text: The vinylic C–H is the weakest, so Br replaces it.
options.explains: Vinylic C–H bonds are strong and their radicals aren't resonance-stabilized. The allylic H is the weak one.

options.text: Light makes the bromonium ion open the other way.
options.explains: No bromonium ion forms here. Light starts a radical chain, which substitutes at the allylic carbon.
